messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 78
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Potter
- Trauma Type: Assault
- Pcl5: 60

She is seventy-eight years old, a potter for sixty-six of those years, and she tells me this as if the number itself is a kind of proof—proof that she knows clay, knows how to center it, knows the feel of wet earth spinning under her palms. She learned from her grandmother in a small village, before she married, before she came to this city, before her husband died. She speaks of those early mornings at the wheel with a softness that is almost gone now. It has been three months since the assault.

She was walking home from the market. It was late afternoon, she says, but still light. A young man grabbed her bag from behind. She did not let go. He pulled harder, and she fell backward, her hip striking the pavement, the back of her head hitting the curb. The bag tore. He ran. A passerby helped her up. She had a small cut on her scalp, a bruise that spread across her hip like a dark bloom. The police came, but he was never found. She tells me this story in the same flat tone she might use to describe a pot that collapsed on the wheel—an accident, a loss, something that simply happened.

But her body tells a different story. Her hands, which have centered thousands of pounds of clay, now tremble when she reaches for the lump. She cannot bear to sit at the wheel. Twice she tried—the first time, her heart pounded so hard she thought she might faint. The second time, she threw a small bowl but then smashed it against the floor. She did not clean up the pieces. They are still there, she tells me, scattered on the studio floor. She has not gone back in a week.

She no longer walks to the market. Her daughter brings groceries every Saturday. She avoids the street where it happened, even though it is the most direct route to the church she has attended for thirty years. She has stopped going to church. She says she does not want to run into anyone who might ask questions. She stays inside. She checks the front door lock three times before bed, then again after she lies down. She sleeps with the hallway light on. She wakes from dreams in which she is falling, always falling, with no ground beneath her.

She startles when the phone rings. She startles when her neighbor knocks. She finds herself scanning the faces of young men on the rare occasions she steps outside, searching for a face she cannot quite remember. The memory of the assault comes to her in fragments—the weight of the bag pulling, the heat of the pavement on her skin, the smell of exhaust and dust. She tries to push these fragments away, but they return when she least expects them: while washing dishes, while sitting in her chair, while trying to pray.

She used to find prayer easy. She used to find pottery easy. Now she sits in her living room and watches the afternoon light move across the floor. She tells me she feels like a pot left too long on the shelf—dried out, cracked, no longer useful. She does not cry when she says this. She says it as fact.

Her daughter says she is not the same woman. She agrees, though she cannot explain what changed. She only knows that the wheel used to be her center, and now the center will not hold. She wants to go back to her studio. She wants to feel the clay again. But every time she tries, she sees the curb, she feels the fall, and she stops. She tells me she does not know what to do with her hands anymore.
